# Redpanda [![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/documentation-black)](https://redpanda.com/documentation) [![Slack](https://img.shields.io/badge/slack-purple)](https://redpanda.com/slack) [![Twitter](https://img.shields.io/twitter/follow/redpandadata.svg?style=social&label=Follow)](https://twitter.com/intent/follow?screen_name=redpandadata) [![Redpanda University](https://img.shields.io/badge/Redpanda%20University-black)](https://university.redpanda.com/)

Redpanda is the most complete, Apache Kafka®-compatible streaming data platform, designed from the ground up to be lighter, faster, and simpler to operate. Free from ZooKeeper™ and JVMs, it prioritizes an end-to-end developer experience with a huge ecosystem of connectors, configurable tiered storage, and more. # Table of Contents - [Get started](#get-started) - [Prebuilt packages](#prebuilt-packages) - [Debian/Ubuntu](#debianubuntu) - [Fedora/RedHat/Amazon Linux](#fedoraredhatamazon-linux) - [macOS](#macos) - [Other Linux environments](#other-linux-environments) - [Build manually](#build-manually) - [Release candidate builds](#release-candidate-builds) - [RC releases on Debian/Ubuntu](#rc-releases-on-debianubuntu) - [RC releases on Fedora/RedHat/Amazon Linux](#rc-releases-on-fedoraredhatamazon-linux) - [RC releases on Docker](#rc-releases-on-docker) - [Community](#community) - [Resources](#resources) # Get started ## Prebuilt packages Redpanda Data recommends using the following free, prebuilt stable releases. ### Debian/Ubuntu ``` curl -1sLf \ 'https://linux.pkg.redpanda.com/setup-redpanda.deb.sh' \ | sudo -E bash sudo apt-get install redpanda ``` ### Fedora/RedHat/Amazon Linux ``` curl -1sLf \ 'https://linux.pkg.redpanda.com/setup-redpanda.rpm.sh' \ | sudo -E bash sudo yum install redpanda ``` ### macOS Download the `rpk` [binary here](https://github.com/redpanda-data/redpanda/releases). Docker is required on MacOS. ``` brew install redpanda-data/tap/redpanda && rpk container start ``` ### Other Linux environments To install from a `.tar.gz` archive, download the file and extract it into `/opt/redpanda`. For amd64: ``` curl -LO https://vectorized-public.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/releases/redpanda/25.2.7/redpanda-25.2.7-amd64.tar.gz ``` For arm64: ``` curl -LO https://vectorized-public.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/releases/redpanda/25.2.7/redpanda-25.2.7-arm64.tar.gz ``` Replace `25.2.7` with the version you want to download. See [Release Notes](https://github.com/redpanda-data/redpanda/releases) for available releases. ## Build Manually Redpanda Data uses [Bazel](https://bazel.build/) as the build system. Bazel automatically manages most of the toolchains and third-party dependencies. We rely on [bazelisk](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazelisk) to get the right version of bazel needed for the build. You can for example install it as follows and add it to your $PATH (or use one of the other suggested ways from their repo). ``` wget -O ~/bin/bazel https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazelisk/releases/latest/download/bazelisk-linux-amd64 && chmod +x ~/bin/bazel ``` There are a few system libraries and preinstalled tools our build assumes are available locally. To bootstrap and build redpanda along with all its tests. ```bash sudo ./bazel/install-deps.sh bazel build --config=release //... ``` For more build configurations, see `.bazelrc`. ## Release candidate builds Redpanda Data creates a release candidate (RC) build when we get close to a new release, and we publish it to make new features available for testing. RC builds are not recommended for production use. ### RC releases on Debian/Ubuntu ```bash curl -1sLf \ 'https://linux.pkg.redpanda.com/setup-redpanda-unstable.deb.sh' \ | sudo -E bash sudo apt-get install redpanda ``` ### RC releases on Fedora/RedHat/Am

historicalFixesSummary.subject: bazel: fetch pip wheels via the Bazel downloader
historicalFixesSummary.body:
rules_python's whl_library shells out to a vendored pip to download wheels,
which fails frequently when PyPI's CDN (files.pythonhosted.org) returns 502s.

Between 2026-08-15 and 2026-08-18 this accounted for 90 of the 347 failed
jobs in the redpanda and vtools pipelines, 58 of them in whl_library.

Setting experimental_index_url switches whl_library to its rctx.download
branch and skips pip for wheel fetching: effective bazel will do the
download in the "bazel way": this means it gets cached through bazel-remote
via the asset cache feature (which we recently turned on).

--require-hashes goes away: it was effectively unused as rules_python strips it,
and it can break for "source dist" libraries, which we don't currently
materialize in the build but which exist in our build. The hashes are
already checked in the lockfile.

Fixes CORE-17093

historicalFixesSummary.subject: config: Lower default fallocate step
historicalFixesSummary.body:
On multiple instances we have now seen heavy XFS fragmentation caused
primarily by small segments as a result of compaction.

This results in XFS extent distributions such as this one:

```
xfs_db -r /mnt/foo -c "freesp -s"
   from      to extents  blocks    pct
      1       1  219159  219159   2.95
      2       3   73640  167835   2.26
      4       7   63231  257920   3.47
      8      15  493848 6637298  89.21
     16      31    9623  157998   2.12
     32      63       3     123   0.00
total free extents 859504
total free blocks 7440333
average free extent size 8.65654
```

The average extent here is just 8 * 4096 bytes so fairly small. Together
with our default fallocate step size of 32MiB this means that when
fallocating XFS has to do a long search to find enough extents. This
basically works by doing repeated finds until enough extents are found
to fulfill the requested 32MiB (these don't have to be contiguous).

We have seen fallocate times up into many hundreds of milliseconds:

```
172.433 (793.406 ms): syscall-8/3970399 fallocate(fd: 748, mode: 17, len: 33554432)
145.233 (820.742 ms): syscall-3/3970403 fallocate(fd: 919, mode: 17, len: 33554432)
180.920 (785.227 ms): syscall-12/3970407 fallocate(fd: 626, mode: 17, len: 33554432)
427.525 (541.225 ms): syscall-11/3970400 fallocate(fd: 614, mode: 17, len: 33554432)
```

fallocates run from the syscall thread. This causes a problems in two
ways. First, any write that is queued logically from the application
level after the fallocate will get massively delayed. Second, any other
unrelated write that got punted to the syscall thread for fallback
reasons will also suffer this latency.

This latency results in both bad Kafka latency and in the worst case can
lead to heartbeat timeouts (which will result in leadership transfers,
new segments, more fallocates and hence a cycle of death).

To avoid these stalls we lower the default falloc step size to 2 MiB.
This has shown to work well in production as well as in manual testing.

Fragmentation like above is easy to reproduce using the XFS punch-holes
script from TCI.

Note that from a manual microbenchmark test it seems like the time it
takes to fallocate scales linearly. fallocate of (N * 10) takes about the
same amount of time as 10 * fallocate(N). So the improvements seem to be
coming from avoiding traditional stop-the-world pauses and pacing via
smaller stalls.

In the good case this seems to have very little to no difference on
performance. A BLB report using an even lower 1MiB step size can be
found here:
https://perf-team-public.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/reports/fallocate.html

An alternative approach would have been to switch from `fallocate` to
using XFS extent size hints. Extent size hints make the larger
allocation happen only at write time. At the same time, it's only a
hint. If only less contiguous space is available then only that amount
will be pre-allocated.

This has a few consequences which make it less appropriate for our usage
or at least could have many hidden consequences:

 - Allocation only happens at write time: This delays disk usage.
   So running out of disk is only noticed later. While this could be a
   pro it's probably more a con for being less predictable.
 - The actual fallocation step size is adaptive in redpanda: fallocation
   step behaviour is adaptive depending on remaining disk usage and
   partition count. Because a just created segment won't allocate any
   space with the extent size hint this means that the adaptive logic
   won't know about live segments until after those start to actually
   use disk. Further, the hinted size can't be changed if extents with
   other sizes exist for a file.
 - We do somewhat want batching in fallocate: Even under fragmentation
   we don't just want to preallocate 8KiB or similar (as might be the
   case with only using the hint). This would cause many many syscall
   thread roundtrips which are worse than doing a medium sized batched
   pre-allocation to amortize the cost across follow-up writes.

The last point could potentially be worked around with by a combination
of first doing a (larger) hinted write followed by fallocating a smaller
chunk and repeating this pattern whenever the multiple of fallocate step
size reaches the hint size. I haven't tested this though as it doesn't
really seem worth it given that the smaller default step size doesn't
seem to have any drawbacks.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: security/audit: report misconfigured auth from client init
historicalFixesSummary.body:
_misconfigured was set only when create_internal_topic() failed, because
that is the one configuration step whose errors reach the kafka client's
mitigate_error(). That step runs only when the local topic table has no
audit topic yet, so reporting a misconfigured authorization raced with
topic table recovery at startup. Every other step, _client.connect()
included, reports its error to do_configure().

Set the flag in do_configure() when any configuration step fails, and
clear it there once every step succeeds. While the flag is set,
audit_log_manager warns on every audit event and applies
audit_log_reject_policy to it.

Covered by audit_log_test.test_no_auth_enabled, which waits for the
rejection warning after removing authentication from a listener.

Signed-off-by: Oren Leiman <oren.leiman@redpanda.com>

before all but the first of its 46 `bazel run` invocations,
warning each time:

  WARNING: Repository '@@rules_python++python+python_3_12_aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu'

historicalFixesSummary.subject: utils: fix unbounded chunked_kv_cache index growth
historicalFixesSummary.body:
The index was reclaimed by walking a single fifo of evicted entries,
stopping at the first entry still on the ghost queue. Main-queue
evictees never enter the ghost queue and were interleaved behind
ghosted entries, and the ghost clock only advances on small-queue
evictions, so under a touch-heavy workload with never-repeating keys
(e.g. the fetch read coalescer) gc stalled behind one live ghost entry
and the index grew by one entry per insertion.

Erase main-queue evictees from the index at eviction time. This leaves
the ghost fifo holding only ghost-queue entries, whose expiry is
monotone in fifo order, making the gc early-return correct.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: k/s: add a deterministic subscription-metadata hash
historicalFixesSummary.body:
A group's assignment depends on the metadata of the topics it subscribes
to. The group stores a hash of that metadata, and a fresh hash that
differs from the stored one bumps the group epoch.

The algorithm is Kafka's KIP-1101: one hash per topic, and one hash for
the group over the per-topic hashes in order of ascending topic name.
The value stays inside one Redpanda cluster, so the byte encoding is
this module's own: fixed-width big-endian integers, and a length before
every string.

Signed-off-by: Oren Leiman <oren.leiman@redpanda.com>

historicalFixesSummary.subject: bazel/seastar: shuffle task queue in non-release builds
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Shuffling was on in our debug CMake builds: Seastar defines
SEASTAR_SHUFFLE_TASK_QUEUE for its Debug, Sanitize and Fuzz
configurations, where swapping pending tasks surfaces latent ordering
assumptions. The move to Bazel dropped it.

@seastar//:shuffle_task_queue becomes tri-state: "auto" (the default)
follows @seastar//:debug, while "true"/"false" force it either way, e.g.
to shuffle in a release build.

.bazelrc sets @seastar//:debug for every build except --config=release,
so fastbuild gets shuffling too. That is deliberate: developers hit bad
ordering assumptions during ordinary local iteration rather than only
under --config=debug in CI.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: rpk: consolidate plugin version validation on pkg
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Define the semver pattern once in pkg/redpanda:
VersionFromString parses versions from command
output, and a new ValidVersion strictly validates
user-supplied flags. The connect, ai, check, and
k8s install commands drop their private regexes
and delegate to ValidVersion.

The parser now accepts any prerelease or build
suffix, so upgrade can parse any version that
install accepts. The ai, check, and k8s
validators previously capped segments at two
digits and accepted trailing garbage; both bugs
are gone with the shared pattern.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: Merge pull request #31411 from bartoszpiekny-redpanda/CORE-15822-audit-skip-create-topic
historicalFixesSummary.body:
[CORE-15822] security/audit: make audit initialization controller-leader independent

Audit-log initialization no longer requires an elected controller leader on either sink, closing the CORE-15822 incident class (init wedged → per-shard queues fill → with audit_failure_policy=reject a cluster-wide authn outage).

RPC sink: skip CreateTopics when the audit topic already exists in the local topic table. Kafka-client sink: propagate the __auditing credential to all brokers up front via inform-all (propagation no longer rides on the create's SASL failure, which also fixes a wedge where a credential minted while peers were unreachable could never propagate), skip the controller-dependent ACL write when both bindings exist locally, skip CreateTopics likewise, and fail initialization loudly on in-band create_acls errors instead of discarding them. A missing-ACL state now surfaces as misconfigured-authorization (topic_authorization_failed) instead of silently dropping records.

Verified by ducktape on both transports: a broker restarting into a leaderless controller window initializes through the skips and an event audited during the window is consumed back from the audit topic while the controller is still leaderless; a genuinely deleted topic is recreated (the skip does not misfire); re-enable with the topic present skips creation and still delivers.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: storage: kill broker process if log_reader detects a corrupt segment
historicalFixesSummary.body:
In cases where a segment file had a zeroed batch header mid-file, the
log reader would return the batches before it and then report a clean
end of stream at the broken header. The offset translator, seeing a
successful read that stopped short of the log tip, would then throw out
of consensus::start(), causing the raft group to never register on that
shard.

log_reader should fail there instead of passing the fault up as a
success. The stream passed to the continuous_batch_parser in
log_segment_batch_reader::initialize is limited by the filesize at
construction, which will match get_stable_offset(). recover_segments
sets stable_offset for each segment from the index (written only after
flushing the appender) or from recovering the segment. Thus, reads up
through the segment's stable offset must succeed -- invalid or missing
batches indicate either a redpanda bug or a fault in the underlying
storage. In either case, we don't want to propagate that state to
clients or other brokers.

consume()'s result<size_t> will report success if any data is read (and
for some errors if no data is read). We need to use error() to see the
actual error result. We also need a bit of additional information to
distinguish a correct end_of_stream from a premature one -- capture
_stable_at_stream_start at continuous_batch_parser construction time
in initialize() and use it to check whether an end_of_stream from
consume() occurred prematurely. The other errors are automatically
fatal as they indicate invalid batches in a range that must be valid.

By default, detecting a fault in a segment kills the broker process as
continuing to operate with a corrupt storage layer is dangerous. Setting
storage_abort_on_corrupt_segment to false will disable this abort and
allow the broker to tolerate the problem. It is a node property because
it must be settable on a broker that will not start.

The following read paths may hit this case:

- kafka fetch, including fetch from a follower
- raft recovery, feeding a lagging follower from the leader's log
- offset translator startup sync
- tiered storage upload
- suffix truncation's offset-to-filepos scan
- compaction, via create_segment_full_reader

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

historicalFixesSummary.subject: sr: log the real cause behind /schemas/ids 403s
historicalFixesSummary.body:
A missing schema id is answered with the same 403 as a genuine ACL
denial so clients can't probe which ids exist, which leaves the broker
log ambiguous during triage. Log the actual cause server-side before
throwing; the client-visible response is unchanged.

Also log (at debug) how many subjects GET /subjects filtered out of
the response for the principal, the same ambiguity in list form.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: rptest: add self-test for OOM crash reporting
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Run a node out of memory via the new oom crash type and check that the
harness reports the failure as a NodeCrash (the crash diagnostic),
rather than a BadLogLines exception triggered by the seastar memory
diagnostics the allocator dumps at ERROR level on the way down: that
dump is on the default log allow list.

In debug builds, which use the system allocator, the oom crash type
refuses to run (it would exhaust host memory rather than hit the
seastar memory limit), so there the test checks the refusal and that
the node survives.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: admin: add oom crash type to /trigger_crash
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Allocate memory in a loop until the seastar allocator fails: ducktape
tests always run with --abort-on-seastar-bad-alloc, so the failing
allocation dumps the seastar memory diagnostics and aborts the process,
reproducing what happens when redpanda runs out of memory in a test.
Chunks are kept small to avoid oversized allocation warnings.

With the system allocator (e.g. debug builds) there is no seastar
memory limit and unbounded allocation would exhaust host memory, so the
endpoint refuses the request in that case.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: bazel: Apply Wno-backend-plugin to abseil crc_x86_arm_combined.cc
historicalFixesSummary.body:
We were seeing:

```
error: external/abseil-cpp+/absl/crc/internal/crc_x86_arm_combined.cc: Function _ZNK4absl12lts_2025081412crc_internal12_GLOBAL__N_145CRC32AcceleratedX86ARMCombinedMultipleStreamsILm1ELm2ELNS2_14CutoffStrategyE1EE6ExtendEPjPKvm is annotated as a hot function but the profile is cold [-Werror,-Wbackend-plugin]
```

`CRC32AcceleratedX86ARMCombinedMultipleStreams::Extend` is marked
`__hot__`.

However, it's a template with non-type template parameters which are
chosen based on the host CPU type.

In training naturally only ever one of those instantiations gets trained
on. The others stay cold.

LLVM emits a warning when a function marked `__hot__` has cold profile
data.

With our new -Werror in external files this caused a build failure.
Silence the warning in that file to fix the build.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: Merge pull request #31461 from bartoszpiekny-redpanda/CORE-14329-test-node-operations
historicalFixesSummary.body:
[ CORE-14329] tests/node_ops: tolerate chaos testing in decommission progress check

NodeDecommissionWaiter.wait_for_removal asserts that a decommission has
"stopped making progress" if replicas_left/bytes-left-to-move hasn't
improved within progress_timeout. In tests that run
FailureInjectorBackgroundThread alongside node operations (e.g.
ShadowLinkingRandomOpsTest.test_node_operations), this assertion can trip
even though the system is behaving correctly: the partition balancer
legitimately stalls while nodes are being restarted, because each restart
resets the ~30s disk-report freshness wait the balancer needs before it can
compute new moves. FailureInjectorBackgroundThread's default cadence
(20-40s between injections) is faster than that recovery window, so a static
progress_timeout can't distinguish "still recovering from ongoing chaos"
from a genuine stall.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: metrics: remove one-shot IMDS connect probe
historicalFixesSummary.body:

bounded base_transport connect before issuing any request. That was a
workaround for client::get_connected retrying in a tight no-backoff loop

the request path no longer spins on an unreachable endpoint. The probe

query_ec2_instance_type's normal failure path. Drop the probe.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: tests/node_ops: tolerate ongoing chaos testing in decommission progress check
historicalFixesSummary.body:
The previous "poll a stable node for decommission status" fix (removed
here) was based on an unconfirmed hypothesis about non-monotonic
replicas_left from random node polling; log analysis of real CI
failures found no evidence for it.

The actual cause of "stopped making progress" false failures is that
the partition balancer legitimately stalls while FailureInjector is
actively restarting nodes: each restart resets the ~30s disk-report
freshness wait the balancer needs before it can act again, and
FailureInjectorBackgroundThread's default cadence (20-40s) is faster
than that recovery window, so a static progress_timeout can't
distinguish "still recovering from chaos" from a genuine stall.

Track failure-injection timestamps on FailureInjectorBackgroundThread
and use them in NodeDecommissionWaiter to hold off the "stopped making
progress" check while chaos has been active in the last
chaos_settle_sec (120s default), with an absolute_max_wait_sec (900s
default) backstop so a genuine deadlock still fails in bounded time.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: hashing/tests: benchmark the crc32c backends
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Compares the google/crc32c and abseil backends of basic_crc32c across
the call patterns redpanda actually uses: bulk contiguous buffers, the
12 incremental integer extends of model::internal_header_only_crc,
fragmented iobufs, and a checksum fused with a copy (abseil's
MemcpyCrc32c, which has no wrapper equivalent and is benchmarked raw).
Both sides go through basic_crc32c, so each backend is measured
exactly as production calls it. Each fixture cross-checks that the two
backends agree before measuring.

Sizes are paired around google/crc32c's block tiers, which it enters
only at 3*336, 3*1360 and 3*5440 bytes. Whatever does not fill a tier
falls to a smaller one and finally to a serial loop, so its throughput
sawtooths by ~15% across a 64 byte change in length and a single size
can rank the two implementations either way.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: storage: keep segment_set formatting bounded under fmt
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Since the fmt 9 upgrade, formatter resolution for segment_set selects
fmt/ranges.h's range formatter over the ostream operator<<, printing
every segment and silently bypassing the 8-segment truncation added in
2023 for this same problem. On partitions with thousands of segments,
formatting a log handle (e.g. "Removing: {}" in log_manager::remove)
then builds a multi-megabyte string in one contiguous fmt buffer, which
can fail allocation on a fragmented shard and abort the process; the
allocation failure report is itself suppressed by the logger's
re-entrancy silencer, so such crashes appear as bare SIGABRTs. Move the
truncation into a format_to member and add an explicit full
fmt::formatter specialization, which takes precedence over any partial
specialization, so no future fmt upgrade or include change can route
around the bound; operator<< now delegates to it. The new gtest covers
the fmt dispatch path (the one that regressed) and asserts ostream
output stays identical.

which are not warning-clean and where -Werror can also break
configure feature checks.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: ct: Fix seen/apply window divergence
historicalFixesSummary.body:
In the ctp_stm::fence_epoch do not demote write lock to read lock.
Old behavior: if the epoch advances the seen window the write lock is
acquired first. This means that all in-flight requests are committed.
The problem is that after demotion the produce request that advances
the seen window may still be scheduled concurrently with a request
that carries previous epoch. There is a very slight room for them
to be reordered and it was never observed but it is still possible.

The fix is to avoid demoting the lock from write to read. The
fence_epoch now returns a fence that carries a write lock if the request
advances the "seen" window.

This may potentially create a performance regression. To avoid this
the second part of this commit (frontend.cc) releases units early.
The units are released when the placeholder is enqueued into Raft. At
this point the reordering of placeholders becomes impossible and it is
safe to release the fence. This allows us to use full write lock in the
fence if needed. The units are only being held up until the placeholder
is queued which is a low latency in-memory operation that doesn't
require any I/O.

The final bit of this PR addresses the failed replication problem.
Currently, if the placeholder replication fails the seen and apply
windows diverge. When the fence is acquired the seen window is advanced
before the placeholder is replicated and applied to the in-memory state
of the STM. After that the background fiber of the ctp_stm applies the
placehodler to the in-memory state and advances the applied window.
When the replication of the placholder fails we can't roll-back the
changes to the seen window because the placeholder could still be
replicated and applied. The replication failure doesn't invalidate all
queued placeholders after the failed one. So, because of that we may
or may not end up in the incorrect state.

To avoid this problem the frontend.cc triggers leadership step down
after a failed replication. This only happens if the placeholder that
moved seen window failed to replicate.

Signed-off-by: Evgeny Lazin <4lazin@gmail.com>

historicalFixesSummary.subject: kvstore: fail fast on flush fiber exceptions
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Exception hygiene: any non-shutdown exception escaping roll() or
flush_and_apply_ops() (e.g. disk I/O errors from segment or snapshot
files) was discarded with the backgrounded future, silently
terminating the flush fiber while the kvstore kept accepting puts
whose futures would never resolve.

Switch to ssx::repeat_until_gate_closed and terminate on non-shutdown
exceptions: mid-flush state cannot be safely retried in-process,
on-disk state is crash-safe, and fail-stop matches the segment
appender's existing policy.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: security/audit: skip audit topic creation when the topic exists
historicalFixesSummary.body:
create_internal_topic() unconditionally sent CreateTopics to the
controller, so every audit enable/startup depended on controller
availability even when the audit topic already existed. In two analyzed
production incidents (CORE-15822, CORE-12785) the topic existed and the
produce path was viable the whole time, yet the audit client looped on
this step forever, which left the audit queues undrained and rejected
authentication cluster-wide.

Check the local topic table first and skip creation when the topic is
already known. RPC sink only: in the Kafka-client sink the create step
doubles as the ephemeral-credential bootstrap -- its SASL failure is
what triggers inform() to the brokers -- so skipping it there leaves
the client unable to authenticate. A stale-negative table read falls
back to the old path; a stale-positive read (topic deleted mid-enable)
has the same exposure as today's create-then-delete race.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: k/s/group_metadata: add the KIP-848 ConsumerGroup* records
historicalFixesSummary.body:
The persisted record types for consumer-protocol groups, lifted from
Kafka's coordinator record schemas and named by the record type their key
version carries:

- 3, consumer group metadata: the group epoch, and the hash that detects
  subscription-metadata changes
- 5, consumer group member metadata: a member's subscription, rack, and
  chosen assignor
- 6, consumer group target assignment metadata: the group epoch the
  current target assignment was computed at
- 7, consumer group target assignment member: the partitions the assignor
  wants a member to own
- 8, consumer group current member assignment: how far a member has
  converged on its target, and what it still owes

Key version 4 is absent: Kafka deprecated ConsumerGroupPartitionMetadata
in favour of the metadata hash, and Redpanda never writes it.

These sit beside the classic records on __consumer_offsets and share the
key-version discriminator, but are framed differently. A key is prefixed
with its record type and is not flexible. A value is prefixed with its
own version and is flexible, so it carries compact strings and arrays
plus a trailing tagged-fields section. Every value keeps unknown_tags so
a tag from a newer writer survives a round-trip.

Decoding that section rejects three things:

- a tag count too large to fit even at two bytes per entry
- a payload size larger than the bytes remaining, which matters because
  consume_unknown_tag allocates the length off the wire before anything
  bounds-checks it
- tag ids that repeat or do not ascend

The new key versions also force both switches over group_metadata_type to
handle them. The classic parsers skip these records, since the state
belongs to consumer_group_stm. For group_tx_tracker_stm that is required
rather than tidy: handle_raft_data has no exception guard and the key
decoder throws on an unknown version, so a ConsumerGroup* record would
otherwise propagate out of do_apply and break tx tracking for the whole
partition.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: rpk/connect: don't cap version segments at two digits
historicalFixesSummary.body:
install validated --connect-version against
`^v?\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}\.\d{1,2}`. The two-digit cap on each segment
rejected every Redpanda Connect release since 4.100.0 before the plugin
manifest was ever consulted.

Segments are now unbounded in width, and the pattern is anchored at both
ends so trailing garbage fails validation up front rather than at
download time. The optional [-+] suffix group preserves prereleases like
4.102.0-rc1, which the previous unanchored pattern accepted and forwarded
to the manifest.

The ai, check and k8s plugin validators carry a copy of the same regex
and are deliberately left untouched here.

Covered by a new TestValidateVersion; the package had no test file
previously.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: cloud_topics: read manifest config from topic table
historicalFixesSummary.body:
The upload loop is signaled from the topic table properties delta but
read the config from the partition's cached copy, which controller
backend updates asynchronously during reconciliation. When the read
won the race, the manifest was uploaded with stale properties,
reported success and was never re-signaled, so a property update
could be missing from the manifest until the next leadership change.

Read the authoritative topic table instead. Also guard against a
same-name recreated topic: a loop for the deleted topic could
otherwise upload the new topic's config under the old revision path.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: `kafka`: speed up all-topics offset fetch on the coordinator shard
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Two fixes for the offset fetch path, which shares the group
coordinator shard with offset commits and grows expensive exactly when
that shard is backlogged:

* `has_pending_transaction()` scanned the entire pending offset commit
  map linearly to test membership. With `require_stable` fetches, this
  ran once per fetched partition, making an all-topics fetch O(offsets x
  pending commits) - aka accidentally quadratic(!) during commit
  backlogs, when the pending map is at its largest. Use the map's O(1)
  lookup.
* an offset can only be unstable when a pending commit or an open
  transaction exists; hoist that check to once per request so the common
  non-transactional steady state skips the per-partition stability probe
  entirely.

Benchmarks (release), all-topics offset fetch per request:

```
    case                                before      after
    -------------------------------------------------------
    require_stable, 256 partitions
      vs 512-entry commit backlog     71.23us     5.69us
```

historicalFixesSummary.subject: `security`: replace ACL store contents atomically
historicalFixesSummary.body:
`reset_bindings()` cleared _acls and _prefix_index and then repopulated
them via `ss::do_for_each()`, which can yield. Authorization checks run
on the same shard in those gaps, so the rebuild was observable as an
empty or partially populated store and denied principals that do hold
the ACL. This is not a narrow window, as the store is empty from the
first interleaved check until the rebuild completes, which for a large
ACL set can be on the order of hundreds of milliseconds.

in, so a reader sees either the whole old set or the whole new one.
`_prefix_index` holds references into the `acls_nodes` that `_acls`
owns, so the two must be published together.

- ts_segment_index (ts_object.{h,cc}): object_index over a segment's

historicalFixesSummary.subject: `ct`: clamp timequeries to the kafka start offset
historicalFixesSummary.body:
`l0_timequery()` passed the query's kafka-space min/max offsets straight
to `make_local_reader()`, which addresses the log in raft offset space.
Reconciliation lets the local log be prefix truncated, so after a
`DeleteRecords` request the Kafka start offset can sit far below the
local log start. The storage layer then rejected the reader with "Reader
cannot read before start of the log" and the request died with a dropped
connection. Clamp the lower bound to the local log start (data below it
has been reconciled and is answered by the L1 query) and translate both
bounds into log offset space, mirroring `partition::local_timequery()`.

The answer itself was also unclamped, and `refine_timequery_result()`
scanned it from its base offset, answering an offset below the start
offset (e.g. 0 after trimming to 1000), which a fetch rejects with
`OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE`. Clamp the refinement scan in offset space to the
query's min offset, leaving the timestamp index seek intact, and fall
back to the L0 candidate when the L1 candidate is clamped away entirely.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: `storage`: defer batch cache index removal to background reclaimer
historicalFixesSummary.body:
The batch cache registers a synchronous memory reclaimer, so reclaim
runs inside the seastar allocator on the allocating fiber's critical
path. Erasing each reclaimed batch's entry from the `btree` index
dominated that work. A 4MiB reclaim (the default `reclaim_max_size`) of
small batches performs ~24k individual btree erases. On memory
pressured fetch-heavy clusters this manifested as 70-250ms reactor
stalls with the allocator -> `run_reclaimers()` -> `batch_cache::reclaim()` ->
`btree::erase()` call chain in nearly every stall backtrace.

Reclaim now frees the batch data and invalidates ranges synchronously
(preserving the reclaimer contract), but defers the index erases to
the background reclaimer fiber, which processes them with scheduling
points in between. Ranges awaiting index removal sit on an auto-unlink
pending list drained by the fiber.

Microbenchmark (release, x86_64), reclaiming 4MiB / ~24k small batches:

    test                    previous commit  this commit
    reclaim_sync            1.04ms           3.69us    (-99.6%)
    reclaim_total           1.04ms           1.04ms    (unchanged)
    reclaim_sync_cold       6.18ms           8.55us    (-99.9%)
    get_hit                 163.56ns         162.72ns  (unchanged)
    get_miss                91.57ns          90.32ns   (unchanged)

`reclaim_sync()` is the synchronous portion on the allocation path.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: [CORE-15837] rpk: add --wait and aggregation to decommission
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Add --wait/-w to 'decommission' and 'decommission-status' so the command
blocks until the decommission completes instead of requiring the operator
to poll decommission-status by hand.

While waiting, print an aggregate progress line (percent complete,
partitions remaining, bytes left to move), redrawn in place on a terminal
and on fresh lines when scripted; -d streams the full per-partition table
instead. --wait-timeout bounds the wait (0 means no limit) and
--poll-interval controls the poll cadence. Allocation and reallocation
failures are surfaced inline but do not stop the wait, since the cluster
retries them. On timeout or Ctrl-C the command exits non-zero and notes
that the decommission continues on the cluster.

    $ rpk cluster brokers decommission 4 --wait
    Success, broker 4 decommission started. Waiting for data to move off the broker...
    broker 4: waiting for the cluster to schedule partition movement
    broker 4: 19% complete (9 partitions remaining, 124895323 left to move)
    broker 4: 40% complete (9 partitions remaining, 92303806 left to move)
    broker 4: 80% complete (8 partitions remaining, 18706975 left to move)
    broker 4: 90% complete (2 partitions remaining, 2777670 left to move)
    Node 4 is decommissioned successfully.

command output matching "ERROR ", not the output itself. kafka-topics.sh
emits such lines from two threads: TopicCommand.printException logs the

historicalFixesSummary.subject: kafka/server: reject client-produced control batches
historicalFixesSummary.body:
In cloud topics a bug was flagged where client-produced control batches
end up in an awkward state: we stamp out their keys and replicate them
as placeholders like we do regular client-produced batches.

This is particularly awkward in rm_stm, where we try to parse the
control placeholder's key[1] and fail, since cloud_topics get their keys
stamped out[2] in placeholders. Typically we expect that Redpanda is the
one generating control batches, so control batches aren't expected to be

same behavior to follow suit.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: bazel: raise --remote_timeout to 600s
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Bazel's default --remote_timeout=60s is an absolute deadline per gRPC
call, so a multi-GB CAS upload that can't finish inside 60s is cancelled
and retried from scratch. Our 1.4-2.2 GB bench binaries and packaging
artifacts routinely exceed it, worst when the cache is cold and every
concurrent build is pushing its largest outputs at once.

A/B on a forced full recompile+relink, one arm per timeout value:
60s gave 3 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED at 59.9999s and 8 failed >1GB uploads;
600s gave zero of either.

600s is a ceiling, not a delay: calls that finish quickly are unaffected.
Placed before the user.bazelrc try-import so a local override still wins.

Full analysis in CORE-16940.

Statically linked binaries (mostly benches) are very large: the
biggest bench binaries and the redpanda binary itself reach ~4 GB

(the gRPC upload exceeds its deadline and is cancelled), so their
link actions never get cache hits and CI relinks them on every
build.

Set --dynamic_mode=fully as the default so binaries link against
shared libraries, and pin release builds back to
--dynamic_mode=default (bazel's built-in default, so the release
configuration is unchanged) to keep static linking where the
binaries ship or performance is measured.

There is no recompilation cost: non-opt binaries already link from
the PIC objects built for the (already dynamically linked) test
binaries, so only link actions change. Debug binaries drop from
~4 GB to a few hundred MB.

```
0x00007ffbee6fc814 in __libc_start_main_impl () from /lib64/libc.so.6
0x000055de9ca00025 in _start ()
```

While the crash initally looks like it's related to static init and
allocator reentrancy that is indeed not the issue.

Instead the issue is that rules_rust exports Rust 1.91's LLVM 21
libprofiler_builtins through every rust_library CcInfo. It came before
Clang 23's libclang_rt.profile.a and satisfied the common
__llvm_profile_* symbols, so Clang 23 instrumentation ran against the
LLVM 21 profile runtime.

Clang 23 bumped the raw profile ABI from 10 to 11 and changed
`__llvm_profile_data::Values`.

This collision was latent with Clang 22 because its 64-byte profile
record still matched LLVM 21.

rules_rust previously discussed runtime version mismatches in
https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_rust/pull/1324, while
https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_rust/pull/3958 only detects whether
profiler_builtins exists and still exports it unconditionally.

However there is no upstream fix. Upstream issue raised at:
https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_rust/issues/4178

We work around the issue by finalizing Wasmtime behind
rust_static_library instead. This is the supported foreign-linker
boundary and causes rustc to include only needed runtime objects in
libwasmtime.a. The archive keeps the C API but does not export
__llvm_profile_*; Clang therefore links its matching profile runtime.
The C++ target name and headers remain unchanged.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: tests: run libFuzzer's loop inside the seastar reactor
historicalFixesSummary.body:
The seastar_fuzz harness ran the reactor on seastar's test-runner
thread and spawned a fiber for every input. The per-input fiber setup
halved exec/s, and a vassert died with no report and no artifact:
seastar's SIGABRT handler, installed after libFuzzer's, took it
first. SEGV survived only because seastar cedes it to ASan.

Invert the setup. The target defines main via RP_SEASTAR_FUZZ and
links libFuzzer without its own (reactor = True on
redpanda_cc_fuzz_test). The reactor boots on libFuzzer's thread and
the loop runs inside it, in a seastar thread. Restoring the pre-boot
crash handlers and unblocking the signals libFuzzer handles lets
crashes produce artifacts; leaving SIGINT and SIGTERM with libFuzzer
keeps its interrupt path working. Reactor-boot allocations are exempt
from leak checks: while a fiber runs, LSan cannot see the roots that
own them. Every input is checked for escaped exceptions and abandoned
failed futures. One shard only; arguments after -- go to the reactor.

The alien::message_queue suppression served the old harness's exit
path; the boot exemption covers it now.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: cloud_topics/l1: add a chunked data source
historicalFixesSummary.body:
A generic, header-only data source that fetches a byte range one fixed-size
chunk at a time, lazily, and presents it as a single contiguous stream: only
the chunks a reader actually consumes are fetched, so a read that stops early
never pulls the tail. It is generic over the fetch callable and its error type,
so it is not tied to tiered storage.

A `use_chunk_aligned_reads` bool_class controls where the first chunk starts:
when yes, chunk boundaries are chunk_size aligned so overlapping reads request
identical (position, length) chunks that a downstream cache can dedup; when no,
the first chunk starts exactly at the read's position (for a caller with no
cache to dedup against). It has no default -- every caller states its choice.
get() checks the abort source on every read, so a cancelled read fails loudly
rather than ending as a truncated clean end-of-stream.

Later commits build the reader and the open_object read path on top of this.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: cloud_topics/l1: carry tiered-storage segment metadata in L1
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Add an optional descriptor that lets an L1 object/extent point at a
segment written in the tiered-storage layout -- its original TS
segment/index/tx objects, addressed by ts_path -- instead of a
natively-written L1 object. Both kinds live in the one configured object
bucket; the distinction is the on-object format and path, not a separate
bucket. Metadata/encoding only; no read, write, or delete path consumes it
yet.

- imported_ts_info (object_id.h): the per-segment descriptor -- ts_path,
  delta_offset/delta_offset_end (log<->kafka offset translation),
  segment_term, and last_kafka_offset. Stored split by ownership: ts_path
  on the object row (imported_ts_object_location), delta/term on the extent
  row (imported_ts_segment_info); absent means a native L1 object.
- Thread it through the metastore read/interface types on both backends:
  an optional imported_ts_info on object_response / extent_object_info
  (recomposed from the storage split on read), plus rpc_types and the
  replicated/domain passthrough.
- Encode it: serde-versioned on both backends (object_entry/extent and the
  LSM rows), the LSM debug-serde path, and the ImportedTsObjectLocation /
  ImportedTsSegmentInfo protobufs. Old-version decode defaults to absent.

[CORE-9724] rptest: harden get_version against slow SSH version reads

Deflakes upgrade tests such as
ClusterConfigAliasTest.test_aliasing_with_upgrade.

During RedpandaInstaller.start() the test runs redpanda --version
over SSH to verify the installed binary. On a loaded CI node this call
occasionally does not emit output within the 10s read timeout, so
paramiko raises a read timeout (PipeTimeout -> socket.timeout ->
TimeoutError) and the whole test fails during setup. This was the only
SSH call in the installer setup/download path with a finite read
timeout; the others (mkdir, ln -s, the tarball curl/gunzip, etc.)
pass timeout_sec=None and block indefinitely, which is why the failure
only ever surfaced in get_version.

Bump the per-attempt timeout to 30s and wrap the read in
wait_until_result(retry_on_exc=True) (the same retry idiom already used
elsewhere in the installer) so a transient stall is retried instead of
aborting the test.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: security: zeroize scram credential cache entries
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Cache values are wrapped in a type that securely erases its bytes on
destruction, so eviction, flush, and shutdown all scrub the derived
key through one destructor. The HMAC digest key is held the same way,
rendering residual key digests in freed hash map slots useless for
offline password testing.

get() now shares ownership of the cache entry instead of returning a
bytes copy: the old copy leaked an uncleansed heap allocation of the
stored key on every hit, and a non-owning view would make callers
responsible for avoiding anything that invalidates cache entries.

[CORE-16860] kafka/client: resume consumer group fetch from committed offset

follow-up to the offset_out_of_range: a fresh HTTP Proxy consumer instance 
now resumes from the group's committed offset instead of always restarting 
at the earliest available offset.

kafka/client: resume consumer group fetch from committed offset — at the
start of fetch(), seed every freshly (re)assigned partition's fetch position
from the group's committed offset (committed+1; our commit stores the last
consumed offset). Only initializing partitions are seeded; no OffsetFetch is
issued once positioned. A per-partition OffsetFetch error surfaces (throws)
instead of a silent restart at earliest.
tests/pandaproxy: cover resume-from-committed end-to-end — two ducktape
cases: (1) instance A commits, is removed, a fresh instance B resumes from
committed+1 (with a control group that has no committed offset starting at
earliest); (2) a consumer commits, retention trims the log start past the
committed offset, and a fresh instance resumes from committed, hits
offset_out_of_range, and recovers to the new log start.
This behaves very similarly to the Confluent REST API: committing offset X
resumes the group at X+1.

historicalFixesSummary.subject: kafka/client: resume consumer group fetch from committed offset
historicalFixesSummary.body:
A fresh consumer instance started every assigned partition at the log
start offset (auto.offset.reset=earliest) even when the group had a
committed offset from a previous instance, so a restarted, rebalanced,
or expired REST proxy consumer re-read the whole retained log instead of
resuming where the group left off.

consumer::fetch() now seeds the fetch position of every assigned
partition that has no position yet from the group's committed offset
before fetching, mirroring the Java consumer's updateFetchPositions ->
refreshCommittedOffsetsIfNeeded -> seekUnvalidated (Confluent REST
proxy). Only initializing partitions are seeded: one that already has an
in-RAM position (a same-instance rebalance) keeps it, since that is at
least as recent as the committed offset. When nothing is initializing no
OffsetFetch is issued.

The seeded position is committed+1: our commit stores the last consumed
offset (commit-all stores position-1; an explicit REST commit stores the
client's value), matching the Confluent REST proxy where posting X
resumes at X+1. A partition with no committed offset (-1) is seeded to
earliest, which also marks it initialized so committed is not re-fetched
on every poll. If committed+1 is below the log start after retention,
the fetch hits offset_out_of_range and the existing reseed to log_start
recovers it. A per-partition OffsetFetch error is not swallowed: it
throws so the retry mitigates, rather than silently starting the
partition at earliest.

fetch_session gains has_offset() to distinguish a genuinely-tracked
offset of 0 from an absent one (offset() returns 0 for both).

Adds fetch_session unit tests for has_offset().

historicalFixesSummary.subject: `kafka`: erase `group` before awaiting `shutdown()`
historicalFixesSummary.body:
Concurrent fibers could race and cause multiple callers into
`group::shutdown()`, triggering an assertion failure:

```
seastar/include/seastar/core/gate.hh:160: future<> seastar::gate::close(): Assertion `!_stopped && "seastar::gate::close() cannot be called more than once"` failed.
```

To avoid this problem, always follow the idiom of finding and erasing
synchronously from `_groups` _first_ (so that concurrent fibers will see
a failure on `_groups.find()`) before awaiting `group::shutdown()`.  Do
the same thing in `stop()`, with an `std::exchange()` on the entire
`_groups` container.
